text: Lesson 24 wrote the requirements. Lesson 25 built the ATF coverage those requirements demanded. This final lesson closes the capstone the way a working ServiceNow DevOps engineer actually would: by writing a deployment runbook a second engineer could follow without needing you in the room. A runbook that only makes sense to the person who wrote it isn't a runbook — it's a memory.

The pre-deployment checklist has three items, each independently verifiable, not assumed. First, the Critical Path Test Suite has run in Test and every test passed — a failing or skipped test is a hard stop, full stop. Second, dependencies are sequenced correctly, the same way Chapter 2 covered: a new field commits before the Flow Action that reads it, in that order, through every instance. Third, the Change Request covering this promotion exists, has the ATF result attached as evidence, and has been formally approved by the Change Advisory Board — not pending, not probably fine by Thursday.

The deployment window is chosen around one absolute constraint: the registrar's three peak enrollment weeks are blacked out entirely, no deployments, no exceptions. Outside those weeks, the window is scheduled for a low-traffic time, late evening, midweek, outside add and drop periods, specifically so the people who'd need to respond to a problem are awake and available, not also trying to register for classes themselves.

The rollback plan is written out before the first production deployment and rehearsed on paper, so nobody improvises under pressure. The trigger is specific: a failed ATF re-test against Prod within the first hour, or confirmed student reports of being unable to register for open sections, starts rollback immediately. The mechanism reverts the Git commit and re-promotes the prior known-good version through the same pipeline — never hand-editing Prod, which this entire course has argued against since Chapter 1. And afterward, a short post-incident review checks whether the ATF suite missed something and needs a new test before trying again.

Here's the honest limit of everything built in this capstone. Every ATF test confirms correctness: does registration work, does a full section get rejected properly, does the capacity math return the right answer. None of that says anything about five thousand students hitting the same form in the same ten-minute window during real peak enrollment. A deployment can pass every test, follow this exact runbook, and still slow to a crawl under load that correctness testing never simulated.

That gap — a fully tested, properly deployed application that still breaks under real production traffic — is exactly where the next course picks up. This completes ServiceNow DevOps, Testing and Deployment, course 11 of 14 in the path. Course 12, ServiceNow Performance Troubleshooting, starts right where this capstone's blind spot ends: what happens when real load, not a test suite, hits the application you just shipped.
